Consult Summary:
- Acute asthma exacerbation in the setting of possible viral trigger/allergic atopy, with plan for intensified inhaled therapy, home monitoring, and follow-up.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Wheezy with shortness of breath for 2–3 days, accompanied by cough and fever.
- Timeline: Symptoms began 2–3 days ago; fever noted (approximate 37°C). Patient reports progressive breathlessness with talking; unable to finish sentences at times. Currently not exercising; unable to walk to work.
- Symptom details: Cough present; no sputum production reported; no chest pain; no hemoptysis; no nocturnal awakenings reported.
- Triggers/exposures: History of asthma in childhood with hay fever and eczema; prior inhaler use; asthma previously stopped several years ago (about 3–4 years). Possible pollen/allergen exposure discussed as potential trigger; viral infection suspected as possible precipitant.
- Prior respiratory history: Childhood asthma described as “quite bad”; past inhaler use; occasional hospital visits; no ICU admission.
- Medications (past/recent): Salbutamol inhaler historically used; currently not on a regular controller; past few years of inhaler use mostly as needed. Dose/route/frequency for salbutamol not documented. Regular antihistamine planned; specific agent not documented. No other medications reported.
- Allergies: None reported.
- Social history: Non-smoker. Drinks about one glass of wine every 2–3 days. Lives with partner; works as an engineer; recently working from home or on sick leave due to illness.
- Functional status: Previously able to walk to work; currently limited; cannot currently exercise; able to climb stairs with some difficulty.
- Review of systems: Fever and cough described; no chest pain; no nocturnal symptoms; no dyspnea at rest; occasional difficulty speaking during episodes.
- Pertinent negatives: No chest pain; no bloody sputum; no night-time symptoms reported.

Past Medical History:
- Childhood asthma (historical; variable severity). 
- Hay fever (allergic rhinitis) and eczema.
- No documented ICU admission; occasional hospital visits for asthma in the past.
- No known drug allergies.

Medications:
- Salbutamol inhaler (past/interruptive use; current use not consistently documented). Dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Regular antihistamine planned; agent and dosing not documented.
- No other current medications documented.

Allergies:
- None stated.

Social History:
- Non-smoker.
- Alcohol: approximately one glass of wine every 2–3 days.
- Occupation: Engineer.
- Living situation: Lives with partner.
- Recent/work status: Working from home or on sick leave due to illness.

Family History:
- Not documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Temperature 37°C.
- Examination findings: Not explicitly documented in the transcript.
- Additional notes: Patient reports wheeze and significant dyspnea on exertion; no nocturnal symptoms reported; able to do some activity (stairs, walking) but limited.

Investigations:
- Peak flow monitoring: Not previously performed; plan to prescribe peak flow meter for home monitoring.
- Other tests/imaging: None reported.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation with possible viral trigger; history of atopy (hay fever) supports allergic predisposition contributing to airway hyperreactivity.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Acute asthma exacerbation
    - Supporting: History of childhood asthma; current wheeze/dyspnea; prior albuterol use; clinician framing as an asthma flare.
    - Opposing: Fever present (can occur with viral triggers; not typical of isolated asthma).
  - Viral upper respiratory infection triggering bronchospasm
    - Supporting: Fever (37°C) and cough; recent onset concurrent with dyspnea.
    - Opposing: Fever is low-grade; no other definitive viral signs documented.
  - Allergic asthma/allergic rhinitis interplay
    - Supporting: Hay fever history; atopic background; potential pollen/allergen trigger discussed.
    - Opposing: Specific allergen exposure not identified.
  - Acute bronchitis
    - Supporting: Cough with airway inflammation could accompany bronchitis.
    - Opposing: No sputum production; lack of auscultatory/ imaging confirmation.

- Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation
  - Assessment: Probable asthma flare given history and symptoms.
  - Plan:
    - Increase inhaled short-acting beta-agonist use to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours as needed; ensure proper spacer technique (spacer to be supplied; pharmacist to instruct).
    - Prescribe/arrange peak flow meter for home monitoring.
    - Instruct patient to record peak flow values on waking and in the evening for the next week; discuss results by phone to determine need for additional inhaler/controller therapy.
    - Discuss potential initiation of additional inhaled therapy if persistent symptoms; arrange a follow-up review in about one week.
    - If fever worsens or wheeze deteriorates, contact clinician promptly for further guidance.
    - Consider regular antihistamine to address atopy/allergic component.
  - Follow-up: In-person or tele-review in approximately one week; sooner if symptoms worsen.

- Issue 2: Viral upper respiratory infection triggering bronchospasm
  - Assessment: Possible viral trigger contributing to asthma flare.
  - Plan:
    - Monitor symptoms; continue current asthma management; escalate inhaler use as above if dyspnea worsens.
    - Follow-up to assess evolution of symptoms and need for additional therapy.

- Issue 3: Allergic rhinitis management
  - Assessment: Atopy evidenced by hay fever history; may contribute to airway hyperresponsiveness.
  - Plan:
    - Start regular antihistamine (agent not specified); available from pharmacy.
    - Document plan and adjust as needed based on response and seasonal/allergen exposure.

- General plan items:
  - Education on inhaler technique; spacer use to improve delivery.
  - Pharmacist guidance on spacer use and peak flow measurement.
  - Schedule follow-up review in about one week; call sooner if symptoms worsen.
  - Consider initiation of a controller therapy after review if asthma control remains suboptimal.
